Description: The SOLAR atmosphere is composed of many species, which are populated at different ionization and excitation levels. the upper chromosphere, transition region, and corona are nearly collisionless. consequently, slippage between, for instance, ions and neutral particles, or interactions between separate species, may have an important effect on alfv n WAVES. long-standing issues concern the 1) generation, propagation, and damping of alfv n WAVES, 2) the role of the particle and wave-particle interactions in the weakly collisional chromosphere, and corona and 3) chemical fractionation (the so-called FIRST ionization potential (fip)-effect, which is the relative enrichment of elements with low FIRST ionization potential in the corona). this proposal aims to investigate multi-fluid and multi-species (mfms) effects on the propagation, dissipation, wave-particle interaction of alfv n WAVES in the SOLAR atmosphere, and any resulting chemical fractionation. in order to achieve this goal, we have developed a 3d mfms numerical code (ebysus, martinez-sykora, et AL. 2020) to investigate such effects. ebysus is capable of treating species (e.g., hydrogen, helium, ETC.) and fluids (neutrals, excited and ionized elements) separately, including non-equilibrium ionization, momentum exchange, radiation, thermal conduction, AS well AS other complex processes in the SOLAR atmosphere. our FIRST highly simplified tests with ebysus reveal that high-frequency WAVES CAN DRIVE velocity drifts between ionized species (martinez-sykora et AL. 2020). such velocity drifts CAN be dissipated with collisions, and it is possible that this may play an essential role in maintaining the chromospheric and transition region (tr) heating. in addition, our preliminary tests generate chemical fractionation of elements. it is well known that chemical fractionation occurs in the stellar atmospheres, which amplitude of abundance depends on the fip-effect. the fip-effect is poorly understood, probably originating in the deep chromosphere where the FIRST ionization occurs and carrying its signature through the many layers and magnetic elements of the corona and SOLAR wind. differing element abundances are one of the most robust discriminators of the various types of SOLAR wind. understanding fractionation is thus a critical ingredient in establishing the connectivity between the SOLAR wind and surface. we are proposing to drastically EXPAND the existing highly idealized numerical models BY investigating high-frequency alfv n WAVES in a stratified atmosphere, expanding the number of dimensions, AS well AS including the necessary physics to be representative of the SOLAR atmosphere. we will synthesize chromospheric and coronal spectral lines to compare with observations such AS IRIS mg II, si iv, and o iv spectra, and hinode/EIS upper tr and coronal line spectra, to validate these WAVES' heating role in the chromosphere and tr. furthermore, our models are of GREAT interest to future dkist observations, for revealing the high-frequency WAVES, and possible EUVST observations designed to investigate the fractionation. if this proposal is selected, our research will focus on the energization of the SOLAR atmosphere, which is highly relevant to NASA's strategic objective 1.1: "understand the sun, earth, SOLAR system, and universe" and the SOLAR and heliospheric physics goal "determine how the sun s magnetism creates its DYNAMIC atmosphere.  and "explore and characterize the physical processes in the sun".
